stories.headline: Democrats lock in largest House majority since 1992 after Foxx loses recount
stories.summary: Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated 11-term Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx in North Carolina after a recount, giving Democrats at least 258 House seats to Republicans' 173, the biggest majority either party has held after a national election in about three decades. Hakeem Jeffries, expected to become speaker in January, laid out priorities on affordability, health care and immigration and said there are areas where Democrats could work with President Trump.
stories.why_it_matters: A majority this large lets Democrats pass bills in the House without Republican votes and run investigations from January, which shapes what reaches the president on health care costs, spending and oversight of his administration.
stories.background: Democrats swept the Nov. 3 midterms, flipping dozens of Republican-held House seats; NPR described it as the biggest win for either party in 50 years. A handful of close races took weeks to settle, including Foxx's western North Carolina district, which went to a recount. Foxx chairs the House Rules Committee, which controls how bills reach the floor. Republicans keep control of the House only until the new Congress is sworn in in January, and they have about three weeks of session left to finish work such as a stopgap spending bill.

facts.text: Chuck Hubbard, a Democrat and retired journalist, defeated Rep. Virginia Foxx after a recount, according to projections by CBS News and NBC News.
Democrats have won at least 258 House seats and Republicans at least 173, the largest majority since the 1992 election.
Foxx had served 11 terms and chairs the House Rules Committee.
Jeffries said Democrats would focus on affordability, expanding health care and fixing what he called a broken immigration system, and named areas where they could work with Trump.
House Republicans have about three weeks left in session before Democrats take over, with a stopgap funding measure at the top of their list, The Hill reported.
Before the final races were called, NPR reported that Democrats had flipped 46 Republican-held seats and called the result the largest win for either party in 50 years.

stories.headline: ICE arrest of father and daughter on Seattle jet bridge draws protests
stories.summary: Immigration officers in plain clothes detained a father and daughter on a jet bridge at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday as they boarded an Alaska Airlines flight, and passenger video of the arrest spread widely. ICE said the two are Mexican nationals who overstayed their visas; their lawyer said they were traveling to a family baptism. Protesters marched through the airport on Sunday, and Washington's governor and Seattle's mayor criticized the agents' tactics.
stories.why_it_matters: The arrest shows immigration enforcement reaching into boarding areas of a major airport, which affects travelers and airline crews as well as immigrants, and it is likely to feed the debate over ICE tactics as Democrats take control of Congress.
stories.background: The Trump administration has stepped up immigration arrests nationwide, and arrests at airports have become more common. Washington state's leaders have repeatedly clashed with the administration over enforcement. The Port of Seattle, which runs the airport, has said it has no authority over federal agencies such as ICE operating there. Officers making arrests in unmarked clothing, sometimes masked, has become a flash point in several cities.

facts.text: Officers detained the two passengers on a jet bridge while people were boarding an Alaska Airlines flight on Saturday, and other passengers filmed it.
ICE said the man and woman, both Mexican nationals, were arrested for allegedly overstaying their visas.
A lawyer for the pair said they were traveling to a family baptism.
CBS News reported that some crew members asked to be replaced after the arrest.
The airport's operator said it was 'outraged', and protesters marched through the airport on Sunday.
Washington's governor called federal immigration agents 'out of control', and Seattle's mayor called the tactics 'un-American'.
The Port of Seattle has said it has no jurisdiction over ICE or Customs and Border Protection operations at the airport.

stories.headline: Army invokes emergency rule to detonate explosives in Iowa despite court order
stories.summary: The Army told a court it will use emergency provisions to detonate about five tons of unstable lead-based explosive material at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant near Middletown, going ahead despite a court order that had paused the plan. The detonation is now set for Wednesday. The Army says freezing temperatures could set off an accidental explosion, while environmental groups say the move sidesteps the court and public safety demands.
stories.why_it_matters: Nearby residents face possible lead exposure and evacuations, and the case tests whether the military can use emergency powers to move ahead while a court has a plan on hold.
stories.background: The Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in southeast Iowa stores drums of lead azide, a sensitive explosive used in detonators, that the Army says have become unstable. The EPA granted an emergency permit this month for controlled detonations, and the Army advised some Middletown residents to leave during the blasts. Environmental groups including the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club's Iowa chapter sued over the permit, and a court paused the plan. The Army has now turned to an emergency exclusion to proceed.

facts.text: The Army told a court it would invoke emergency provisions to carry out the detonation despite a court order that had put it on hold.
The Army plans to use an emergency munitions and explosives exclusion to the EPA's permit, according to court records cited by CBS News.
The material is about five tons of bomb-making chemicals; the New York Post put it at 68 barrels of a toxic lead explosive.
The Army rescheduled the detonation for Wednesday to allow for weather and 'mitigation measures,' NPR reported.
The Army has advised residents of Middletown's City Park neighborhood to temporarily leave during detonations.

stories.headline: Appeals court rules pregnant-worker accommodations law unconstitutional
stories.summary: A federal appeals court ruled that the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act, which requires employers to make reasonable accommodations for pregnant workers, is unconstitutional. The court said Congress passed it improperly because most House members were not physically present when it was approved in a December 2022 spending package. The decision is likely headed toward the Supreme Court.
stories.why_it_matters: The law guarantees pregnant workers changes like extra breaks, seating or lighter duty; the ruling puts those protections in doubt for workers covered by it and raises questions about other laws passed under pandemic-era proxy voting.
stories.background: Congress passed the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act in late 2022 as part of a large spending bill, while the House still allowed members to vote by proxy during the COVID-19 pandemic. Texas sued, arguing the Constitution requires a quorum of members to be physically present. A three-judge panel of the 5th Circuit upheld the law in August 2025, but the full court vacated that ruling in January 2026 and reheard the case. The challenge has so far concerned Texas as an employer.

facts.text: An appeals court ruled that the federal law requiring accommodations for pregnant workers is unconstitutional.
The court said the law was invalid because a majority of House members were not physically present when it passed as part of a December 2022 spending package.
The full 5th Circuit had vacated an August 2025 panel decision upholding the law and agreed in January 2026 to rehear Texas's challenge.
At the May 2026 rehearing, conservative judges questioned the Justice Department's argument that physical presence was not required, Bloomberg Law reported.

stories.headline: Delta system failure and coast-to-coast storms snarl start of Thanksgiving travel
stories.summary: A failure in Delta Air Lines' automated system for calculating aircraft weight and balance delayed flights on Sunday, mostly at its Atlanta hub, and prompted a roughly hourlong FAA ground stop for some Atlanta-bound flights. Delta said the problem was resolved, but storms on both coasts are forecast to complicate travel through the holiday week.
stories.why_it_matters: Anyone flying or driving for Thanksgiving this week should expect possible delays, especially through Atlanta, the Northeast and California.
stories.background: Airlines must calculate each flight's weight and balance before takeoff, so when that system fails, departures stall. Sunday's disruption came a week after a nationwide FAA ground stop, caused by a telecommunications outage, canceled thousands of flights. Thanksgiving week is one of the busiest travel periods of the year. Forecasters are watching separate storms bringing rain, flooding and wind to the East and West Coasts.

facts.text: The system that failed calculates the weight and balance of departing flights.
The FAA issued about an hourlong ground stop for some flights into Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, Delta's hub.
Delta said crews used manual workarounds and later said the issue was resolved.
A nationwide FAA ground stop the previous weekend, which the agency blamed on a telecommunications outage, led to thousands of cancellations.
Forecasters warned of strong storms, flooding and high winds in parts of the Northeast and California during Thanksgiving week.

stories.headline: DNC plans 12 debates for 2028 primary, starting June 2027
stories.summary: The Democratic National Committee announced 12 presidential primary debates for the 2028 race, with the first in June 2027. To take part, candidates will have to pledge to denounce spending by supportive outside groups that do not disclose their donors.
stories.why_it_matters: The rules shape which Democrats voters get to see on the debate stage and how much anonymous money can flow into the race to pick the party's next presidential nominee.
stories.background: Debate schedules and entry rules are set by the national party and often decide which candidates gain attention in a crowded field. DNC Chair Ken Martin pushed a resolution in August 2025 to curb corporate and so-called dark money in the 2028 nominating contest. Dark money refers to political spending by groups that do not reveal their donors. The Washington Post reported the June start came after pushback against an earlier date.

facts.text: The DNC plans 12 primary debates across 2027 and 2028, beginning in June 2027.

stories.headline: Trump signals interest after Sen.-elect El-Sayed pitches universal health care as 'TrumpCare'
stories.summary: President Trump responded on social media to Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed's proposal to name a universal health care plan 'TrumpCare' if the president lets it pass, in a post that appeared to leave the door open. El-Sayed said Sunday he is open to working with the administration to lower health costs.
stories.why_it_matters: If the two sides find any common ground, it could affect what Americans pay for health care, though no bill or agreement exists yet. Almost all coverage of the exchange came from left-leaning outlets.
stories.background: El-Sayed, a progressive Democrat and physician, won a Senate seat in Michigan in the midterms after a tense campaign. He supports Medicare for All, a single government-run insurance plan for everyone. He first floated the 'TrumpCare' name in early November, saying the president likes putting his name on things. Trump has recently attacked large insurance companies, and Democrats will control Congress from January.

facts.text: Trump responded on Saturday to El-Sayed's push to call universal health care 'TrumpCare.'
El-Sayed said Sunday he is open to working with Trump to bring down costs and improve health care.
